statutes_cited: Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
Sections 18 and 23 of the Punjab Civil Servants Act, 1974
holding: For the foregoing reasons, all three constitutional petitions are allowed in the above terms. The clarification dated 30.05.2025, bearing No.FD-SR-III-4-237/2024, is declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect insofar as it purports to introduce an independent disqualification, alter the scope of Rule 4.10 or restrict an entitlement contrary to Section 18(2) Act. Likewise, the notifications dated 02.12.2024 and 20.08.2025, whereby amendments were introduced in Rule 4.10 of the Rules, are declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect only to the extent that their provisions are construed or applied so as to exclude otherwise eligible members of the deceased civil servant’s family in a manner inconsistent with Section 18(2) of the Act. Consequently, the impugned communications/orders declining the petitioners’ claims solely on the basis of the aforesaid unlawful restriction are hereby set aside.

paragraphs.text: Syed Ahsan Raza Kazmi, J. Through this single judgment, I intend to decide the instant Constitutional Petition along with connected Writ Petition Nos.3426 of 2026 and 4050 of 2026, as the controversies involved therein arise out of similar facts and give rise to common questions of law.

Through these constitutional petitions, instituted under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as the “Constitution”), the petitioners have called in question the refusal of family pension under the Punjab Date of Hearing 28.10.2026 Petitioner(s) in the titled writ petition and connected Writ Petition Nos.3426 of 2026 & 4050 of 2026 by: M/s. Sardar Bilal, Tahir Malik, Muhammad Muneeeb and Sayyed Umer Sohail Shah, Advocates. Respondents by: Mr. Muhammad Idrees Rafique Bhatti, learned A.A.G. alongwith Adnan Saleem, Senior Auditor, DAO, Rawalpindi Accounts Branch. Civil Services Pension Rules, 1963 (hereinafter referred to as the “Rules”), principally on the basis of notifications and clarification issued by the Finance Department, Government of the Punjab, dated 02.12.2024 and 30.05.2025, respectively, as well as the subsequent amendment notification dated 20.08.2025. The controversy essentially concerns the legality and effect of these instruments insofar as they restrict the entitlement to family pension to the surviving spouse, thereby excluding other members of the deceased civil servant’s family.

Briefly stated, the first petition, i.e. W.P. No.26 of 2026, has been instituted by Zahida Yasmeen, an unmarried daughter of late Shah Nawaz Khan, who was serving as a regular employee of PRTC, Lahore, and died on 23.04.2025. Her claim for family pension was declined by reference to Finance Department Notification No.FD-SR-III-4-244/2023(B), dated 02.12.2024, and the subsequent departmental clarification.

The second petition, i.e. W.P. No.3426 of 2026, has been filed by Mst. Nosheen Malik, a divorced daughter of late Ibrar Hussain, who served as an Assistant in BPS-11 in the Food Department/Punjab Food Authority, retired on 01.01.2002 and died on 13.04.2026. Her mother had predeceased her father. Her claim for family pension was declined through communication/order dated 24.08.2026, by placing reliance upon the amended pension framework and the relevant departmental instruments.

The third petition, i.e. W.P. No.4050 of 2026, has been instituted by Mst. Falak Shah, a divorced daughter of late Rizwana Tasleem, a retired teacher in BPS-16, who died on 27.12.2024, and late Syed Tasleem Ul Islam, a retired employee of the Municipal Corporation, Rawalpindi, in BPS-14, who died on 24.09.2025. The petitioner’s marriage was dissolved through khula on 22.12.2021. She asserts that she has not remarried and has no independent source of income. Her claims relating to the pension of her deceased mother and father were declined through separate communications dated 23.12.2025 and 04.02.2026, respectively, by invoking the impugned departmental instruments.

The common grievance of the petitioners is that their claims have been rejected by applying a restrictive interpretation of the pension framework, which confines family pension to the surviving spouse and excludes daughters irrespective of their status or eligibility under the governing law. Learned counsel for the petitioners contend that Sections 18 and 23 of the Punjab Civil Servants Act, 1974 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”), must be read harmoniously with the Rules. Section 18 recognises the statutory entitlement to pension and family pension, whereas Section 23 empowers the competent authority to frame rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act. Such delegated authority, however, cannot be exercised in a manner that abridges or defeats the substantive entitlement recognised by the parent statute. It is further contended that an executive clarification cannot introduce a disqualification or eligibility condition not contemplated by the Act or the Rules. Reliance has also been placed upon Articles 4, 9, 14, 25, 37 and 38 of the Constitution, the principles of equality and dignity, and the relevant international obligations concerning non-discrimination against women.

Conversely, the learned Law Officer, assisted by the respondents, supports the impugned action on the ground that the Government is competent to regulate pensionary benefits through rules framed under the Act. It is argued that pension is payable strictly in accordance with the law in force and no claimant can insist upon a benefit contrary to the applicable Rules. According to the learned Law Officer, the impugned amendments and departmental instruments were issued by the competent authority in exercise of its lawful powers, keeping in view the financial and administrative requirements of the pension system.

Before examining the controversy on merits, the objection regarding maintainability of these petitions requires consideration. The respondents have questioned the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court by invoking Article 212 of the Constitution, the law governing service disputes and the availability of departmental remedies. The petitioners, however, maintain that their challenge is directed not merely against individual administrative decisions but also against the legality and competence of the instruments under which their claims have been declined.

It has by now been settled that the nature of the controversy and the relief sought, rather than the nomenclature of the proceedings, determine the question of jurisdiction. Article 212 of the Constitution cannot be bypassed merely by incorporating a plea of violation of fundamental rights or challenging an administrative instrument. At the same time, the service-related origin of a dispute does not, by itself, dispense with examination of a properly raised challenge to the competence or legality of the instrument under which the impugned action has been taken. The Court is, therefore, required to examine the precise nature of the challenge, the statutory bar, if any, and the jurisdiction of the alternative forum.

In the present cases, the petitioners have principally questioned the authority of the Finance Department to introduce, through the impugned instruments, restrictions upon the class of beneficiaries recognised under Section 18(2) of the Act. Their grievance is not confined to a factual assessment of their individual pension claims; rather, it raises a question concerning the limits of delegated legislative and executive authority.

The controversy primarily revolves around the interpretation of Sections 18 and 23 of the Act. Section 18(1) recognises the entitlement of a civil servant to pension or gratuity upon retirement, whereas Section 18(2) specifically provides as follows: “In the event of death of a civil servant, whether before or after retirement, his family shall be entitled to receive such pension or gratuity or both as may be prescribed.” A plain reading of the aforesaid provision demonstrates that the Legislature has expressly recognised the family of a deceased civil servant as the beneficiary of the statutory entitlement, leaving the manner and conditions of its payment to be prescribed under the Rules. Section 23 of Act is reproduce hereunder:- Rules (1) The Governor, or any person authorized in this behalf may make such rules as appear to him to be necessary or expedient for carrying out the purposes of this Act. (2) Any rules, orders or instructions in respect of any terms and conditions of service of civil servants duly made or issued by an authority competent to make them and in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall, in so far as such rules, orders or instructions are not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, be deemed to be rules made under this Act Section 23 of the Act empowers the competent authority to frame rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act. Such power, however, is not unfettered and must necessarily be exercised within the limits of the parent enactment. The authority to regulate an entitlement cannot be construed as an authority to defeat or contradict the substantive provision from which that entitlement originates.

Much has been observed on the legal character of the pension by the Superior Courts. Pension, where the prescribed statutory conditions stand fulfilled, is not a bounty dependent upon the discretion or benevolence of the Government. It constitutes a legally regulated entitlement earned through service rendered under the governing law. Its payment may, undoubtedly, be subjected to conditions lawfully prescribed by the competent authority; however, the executive cannot withhold, reduce or extinguish such entitlement through an instrument unsupported by the enabling legislation. The distinction, therefore, lies between regulating the exercise of a statutory right in accordance with law and introducing an additional restriction beyond the authority conferred by the Legislature.

The jurisprudential foundation of this principle has been recognised by the august Supreme Court in the judgment reported as Secretary, Government of the Punjab, Finance Department and 269 others vs. M.Ismail Tayer and 269 others (2014 SCMR 1336), wherein pension was treated as a vested right and a legitimate expectation founded upon the applicable statutory framework. The principle does not place pension beyond lawful regulation; rather, it requires that any restriction, reduction or refusal must have a valid legal foundation and remain within the limits of the governing statute and rules. The same consideration applies to family pension, the entitlement to which must be determined in accordance with the applicable law and cannot be defeated merely through an administrative condition that the competent legislation does not authorise.

The constitutional and social significance of family pension also cannot be overlooked. It may constitute an important source of financial security for a surviving member of the deceased civil servant’s family. Nevertheless, the Court is not concerned with creating an entitlement dehors the governing law, but with ensuring that the statutory expression employed by the Legislature is not narrowed through an administrative interpretation unsupported by the parent enactment.

It is a settled principle of statutory interpretation that where a term is not expressly defined in the parent statute, it must ordinarily be construed according to its natural, ordinary and dictionary meaning, having regard to the context in which it occurs and the object sought to be achieved by the legislation. In the present case, the expression “family” has not been assigned any general or exhaustive definition under Section 2 of the Act. Rather, Section 18(2) recognises the entitlement of the family of a deceased civil servant to pension or gratuity, as may be prescribed under the relevant Rules.

The legislative approach towards the expression “family” is further illustrated by the Punjab Government Employees Welfare Fund Ordinance, 1969, wherein the expression has expressly been defined under Section 2(a) to include spouse, legitimate and stepchildren, and dependent parents, sisters and minor brothers. Similarly, Section 20 of the Act recognises the entitlement of civil servants and their families to benefits under the relevant Benevolent Fund and Welfare Fund legislation, whereas Rule 2(c) of the West Pakistan Government Servants (Medical Attendance) Rules 1959 provides the definition of “family” as “wife/husband, legitimate sons and daughters and step-children of a Government servant, wholly dependent upon him. These provisions demonstrate that the expression “family” has been employed in different welfare-related enactments in a broader sense, according to the nature and object of the benefit concerned. However, a definition enacted for a particular statutory purpose cannot mechanically be imported into another enactment so as to govern or curtail an entitlement arising thereunder. The definition contained in the Welfare Fund Ordinance and the West Pakistan Government Servants (Medical Attendance) Rules 1959 are, therefore, relevant as an interpretive aid.

In the absence of an exhaustive definition in the governing provision, the expression “family” must be construed in its ordinary and natural sense, keeping in view the relationship by blood, marriage or legal affiliation, the dependency of the persons concerned, and the beneficial object of the legislation. The expression cannot, without clear statutory authority, be reduced to mean the surviving spouse alone. Particularly in matters relating to family pension and post-retirement benefits, a beneficial interpretation ought to be preferred, provided it remains consistent with the language, scheme and legislative intent of the governing statute. In this regard, Rule 4.7(1) of the Rules, while dealing with gratuity, refers to the family of a Government servant and includes, inter alia, wife or wives of a male Government servant, husband of a female Government servant, children of the Government servant and widow or widows and children of a deceased son of the Government servant. Although the said provision relates to gratuity and cannot, by itself, be treated as an exhaustive definition governing family pension under Rule 4.10, it does demonstrate that the expression “family” is not invariably synonymous with the surviving spouse alone. Likewise, the ordinary meaning of the expression “family”, as reflected in Black’s Law Dictionary, encompasses persons connected by blood, affinity or law, particularly within a defined generational relationship, and may also refer to a group consisting of parents and their children. Even otherwise where the governing statute employs the wider expression “family”, its scope cannot be curtailed merely by adopting a restricted administrative understanding unsupported by the statutory scheme.

Before the amendment the Rule 4.10 of the Rules is reproduced hereunder:- 4.10 (1) Family for the purpose of payment of family pension shall be as defined in sub-rule (1) of rule 4.7. It shall also include the Government Servant's relatives mentioned in clause (d) of rule 4.8. (2) (A) A family pension sanctioned under this section shall be allowed as under: (i) (a) To the widow of the deceased, if the deceased is a male Government servant, or to the husband, if the deceased is a female Government servant. (b) If the Government servant had more than one wife, and the number of his surviving widows and children does not exceed 4, the pension shall be divided equally among the surviving widows and eligible children. If the number of surviving widows and children together is more than 4, the pension shall be divided in the following manner, viz, each surviving widow shall get 1/4th of the pension and the balance (if any) shall be divided equally among the surviving eligible children. Distribution in the above manner shall also take place whenever the Government servant leaves behind surviving children of a wife that has predeceased him in addition to the widow and her children, if any. (c) In the case of a female Government servant leaving behind children from a former marriage in addition to her husband and children by her surviving husband, the amount of pension shall be divided equally among the husband and all eligible children. In case the total number of beneficiaries exceeds four, the husband shall be allowed 1/4th of the pension and the remaining amount distributed equally among the eligible children. (ii) Failing a widow or husband, as the case may be, the pension shall be divided equal among the surviving sons not above 24 years and unmarried daughters. Note: In working out the share of the various heirs under sub-clause (A) (i) and (ii), the amount should be calculated to the nearest paisa. (iii) Failing (i) and (ii), to the eldest widowed daughter. (iv) Failing (i) to (iii), to the eldest widow of a deceased son of the Government servant. (v) Failing (i) to (iv), to the eldest surviving son of a deceased son of the Government servant. (vi) Failing (i) to (v), to the eldest unmarried daughter of a deceased son of the Government servant. (vii) Failing these, to the eldest widowed daughter of a deceased son of the Government servant. (B) If the family pension is not payable under clause (A), it may be granted: (i) to the father; (ii) failing the father, to the mother; (iii) failing the father and the mother, to the eldest surviving brother below the age of 21 years; (iv) failing (i) to (iii), to the eldest surviving unmarried sister, if the eldest sister married or dies then the next eldest; (v) failing (i) to (iv) to the eldest surviving widowed sister. (3) No family pension shall be payable under this section – (a) to an unmarried female member of a Government servant's family in the event of her marriage; (b) to a widowed female member of a Government servant's family in the event of her re-marriage; (c) to the brother of a Government servant on his attaining the age of 21 years. (d) to a person who is not member of a Government servant's family. (4) A family pension awarded under this section shall not be payable to more than one member of a Government servant's family at the same time except as provided for in sub-clause (A) (i) and (ii) of sub-rule (2) above. (5) (a) If the pension ceases to be granted before the expiry of the period for which it is admissible on death or marriage of the recipient or on account of other causes, to persons falling under sub-clauses (A) (i) and (ii) of sub-rule (2) above, the amount shall be granted to other recipients in equal shares. (b) If a family pension awarded under this section other than that mentioned in clause (A) (i) or (ii) of sub-rule (2) of this rule ceases to be payable before the expiry of the period up to which it is admissible on account of death or marriage of the recipient or other causes, it shall be regarded to the person next lower in order mentioned in sub-rule (2). (6) Government shall have discretion to make such modification in the mode of allotment or conditions of tenure set forth in sub-rules (2) to (5) above as they may consider desirable to suit the special circumstances of the beneficiaries. (7) A family pension sanctioned under this section shall be payable in addition to any extraordinary pension or gratuity that may be granted to the members of a Government servant's family under any other rules in force for the time being. (8) Further good conduct of the recipient is an implied condition of every grant of a family pension under this section. The controversy must now be examined in the context of Rule 4.10 of the Rules, which specifically deals with family pension and has undergone amendments from time to time. Through Notification No.FD-SR-III-4-244/2023(B), dated 02.12.2024, the Finance Department substituted sub-rules (1) to (6) of Rule 4.10 and introduced a framework under which family pension was restricted to the spouse for a period of ten years or until remarriage, whichever occurred earlier, subject to the exception provided therein in respect of an issueless spouse. Thereafter, through clarification No.FD-SR-III-4-237/2024, dated 30.05.2025, the Finance Department explained the implementation of the amended provision. Subsequently, through notification dated 20.08.2025, Rule 4.10(1) was again substituted, providing for family pension to the spouse for life or until remarriage, with provision for equal division amongst widows where there is more than one widow.

The aforesaid instruments, therefore, require examination in their proper statutory perspective. Whereas the communication dated 30.05.2025 is an administrative clarification, the notifications dated 02.12.2024 and 20.08.2025 purport to amend the statutory Rules in exercise of the delegated rule-making power. The legal effect of these instruments cannot be treated as identical. A departmental clarification cannot amend the Rules or independently create a disqualification. As the subordinate legislation cannot alter the principle legislation. This interpretation finds direct support from the judgment of the august Supreme Court in The Province of Punjab through Secretary, Finance Department v. Kanwal Rashid and others (2021 SCMR 730). In the said case, both parents of the respondent were civil servants and, upon their respective deaths, she was receiving family pension in respect of both. The Finance Department, through a departmental clarification, sought to restrict her entitlement to only one family pension and also initiated proceedings for recovery of the amount allegedly paid in excess. The august Supreme Court examined the authority of the Finance Department to issue such clarification and held that the Department had no lawful authority to interpret, abridge or enlarge the right conferred under Section 18(2) of the Act, or to modify Rule 4.10 of the Rules through an administrative clarification. Such an exercise amounted to an assumption of the rule-making power vested in the competent authority under the Act.

The august Supreme Court further held that a departmental clarification could not retrospectively impair a pensionary entitlement which had already accrued and was being regularly received. While examining the distinction drawn between an unmarried son and an unmarried daughter, the Court also held that treating the receipt of one family pension by an unmarried daughter as a regular source of income, thereby disentitling her from the family pension of the other deceased parent, was discriminatory and offended Article 25 of the Constitution. It was clarified that the expression “acquiring a regular source of income” contemplated an independent source of income acquired by the beneficiary through her own efforts; family pension received by virtue of the death of a parent could not, by itself, be treated as such an independently acquired source of income.

The principle emerging from the afore referred judgment is of particular relevance to the controversy before this Court. It establishes that the Finance Department cannot, by issuing an executive clarification, introduce a disqualification or restriction which has the effect of curtailing the statutory entitlement recognised by Section 18(2) of the Act. Nor can the receipt of family pension, merely by reason of its being a pensionary benefit, be treated as an independently acquired regular source of income for the purpose of excluding an otherwise eligible daughter from the benefit available under the governing law.

It is, however, necessary to observe that case of Kanwal Rashid supra dealt with the validity and effect of an administrative clarification under the then prevailing framework. The impugned instruments in the present petitions include not only a departmental clarification but also subsequent formal amendments to Rule 4.10. Their validity, therefore, has to be examined independently in the light of Sections 18(2) and 23 of the Act. The judgment in Kanwal Rashid supra cannot be construed as having directly adjudicated upon the validity of the subsequent amendments. Nevertheless, the governing principle laid down by the august Supreme Court remains binding: neither delegated legislation nor executive instructions can travel beyond the authority conferred by the parent statute or defeat a substantive entitlement recognised therein.

The governing principle is that subordinate legislation may supplement the parent statute but cannot supplant it. In Kanwal Rashid supra, the august Supreme Court specifically examined the authority of the Finance Department in relation to family pension and held that the Department had no authority to clarify, interpret, abridge or extend the right of pension provided under Section 18(2) of the Act and regulated by the Rules. Although the Kanal Rashid judgment concerned a departmental clarification and does not, by itself, determine the validity of every subsequent formal amendment to the Rules, it underscores the controlling force of the parent statute and the limitations upon executive authority.

It is, therefore, necessary to distinguish between an administrative clarification and a formal amendment to statutory rules. A clarification cannot amend the Rules or introduce a condition not contemplated therein. A formal amendment, even when made in exercise of the statutory rule-making power, is equally subject to the limitations of the parent enactment. The mere invocation of Section 23 of the Act does not confer unrestricted authority upon the delegate to alter the substantive scope of the entitlement recognised by Section 18(2).

The principle finds further support from the judgment of the august Supreme Court in Province of Sindh through Secretary, Government of Sindh, Karachi and others v. Mst. Sorath Fatima and another (PLD 2025 SC 856). In the said case, the august Supreme Court disapproved the imposition, through a departmental circular, of a condition making a daughter’s entitlement dependent upon her marital status at the precise time of the pensioner’s death, where such condition was not prescribed by the governing Act or Rules. The principle emerging therefrom is that an executive instrument cannot introduce an additional disqualification or impose a temporal condition which the governing law does not contemplate. This reasoning directly bears upon the clarification dated 30.05.2025. As regards the formal amendments to Rule 4.10, their validity must independently be tested against Sections 18(2) and 23 of the Act.

The legal position that subordinate legislation must remain within the confines of its enabling statute is firmly settled. Rules and regulations derive their authority from the parent enactment and cannot travel beyond the legislative policy embodied therein. The rule-making authority is empowered to supplement the statute for carrying out its purposes, but cannot supplant, contradict or enlarge the substantive provisions of the enactment. Where a subordinate provision is inconsistent with the parent statute, it must yield to the latter. The august Supreme Court has reiterated this principle in the following judgments: In National Electric Power Regulatory Authority v. Faisalabad Electric Supply Company Ltd. (2016 SCMR 550), it was held that rules and regulations are the progeny of a statute and must remain strictly within its precincts. The relevant observation reads as follows: “11…. Rules and or Regulations are the progeny or off spring of a Statute and are to be strictly in conformity with the provisions of the Statute where under same are framed. It is settled proposition of law that the rules framed under a Statute are to remain within the precinct of the Statute itself and cannot transgress the limits and parameters of the parent Statute itself. All efforts are to be made to interpret the rules so as to bring it in conformity and without injuring the intent and spirit of the Statute, where it is not possible then the rules in as much as it is injuring the very intent and spirit which must yield to the Statute.” In Suo Motu Case No.13 of 2009 (PLD 2011 Supreme Court 619), the august Supreme Court held: “18. From an examination of the above case law it is clear that a rule making body cannot frame rules in conflict with, or in derogation of, the substantive provisions of the law or statute, under which the rules are framed. Rules cannot go beyond the scope of the Act. Thus, we are inclined to hold that no rule can be made which is inconsistent with the parent statute, whereas, no regulation can be made inconsistent with the parent statute or the rules made thereunder and the provisions of these rules or regulations, as the case may be, to the extent of their inconsistency with the parent statute or the rules shall be inoperative.” The same principle was reiterated in Suo Motu Case No.11 of 2011 (PLD 2014 Supreme Court 389). In Khawaja Ahmad Hassan v. Government of Punjab (2005 SCMR 186), the august Supreme Court held that a statutory rule cannot enlarge the scope of the section under which it is framed and, where a rule travels beyond what the parent provision contemplates, it must yield to the statute. In Pakistan v. Aryan Petro Chemical Industries (Pvt.) Ltd. (2003 SCMR 370), it was reiterated that the rule-making authority must exercise its powers within the mandate conferred by the Legislature and that rules inconsistent with the substantive provisions of the parent statute are invalid. In Mian Ziauddin v. Punjab Local Government (1985 SCMR 365), it was held that rules framed under an Ordinance cannot travel beyond or overreach the Ordinance itself. In Professor Kazim Hussain v. Government of Pakistan (PLD 2013 Federal Shariat Court 18), it was observed that delegated legislation must remain consistent with the statute under which it is framed and cannot neutralise or contradict the substantive provisions of the enactment. The Lahore High Court, in Independent Newspapers Corporation (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2017 Lahore 289), reiterated that rules and regulations framed under a statute cannot transgress the limits set by the parent enactment and any provision exceeding the delegated authority is liable to be declared illegal.

The cumulative effect of the above discussion is that the rule- making power is ancillary to the parent statute and cannot be employed to defeat the legislative intent or alter the substantive scope of a right conferred by the Legislature. Applying this settled principle to the present controversy, Section 18(2) expressly recognises the family of a deceased civil servant as the beneficiary of the prescribed pensionary entitlement. The power under Section 23 undoubtedly enables the competent authority to prescribe the manner, conditions and procedure governing payment of family pension. However, such power cannot be construed as an unrestricted authority to substitute the statutory expression “family” with “spouse” and thereby exclude the remaining otherwise eligible members of the family, where such exclusion is inconsistent with the parent enactment and the legislative policy embodied therein. At the same time, the expression “family” cannot be construed as conferring an automatic right upon every relative of a deceased civil servant, irrespective of the eligibility requirements lawfully prescribed under the Rules.

Examined in the above perspective, the clarification dated 30.05.2025 cannot independently alter the scope of Rule 4.10, introduce a new disqualification or extinguish an entitlement otherwise available under the governing statutory framework. As regards the formal amendments introduced through notifications dated 02.12.2024 and 20.08.2025, the fact that they were issued in exercise of the rule-making power under Section 23 does not place them beyond judicial scrutiny. The authority to prescribe the manner and conditions of payment does not extend to making a provision which, in substance, defeats the statutory entitlement recognised by Section 18(2). To the extent that the impugned amendments are applied as an absolute exclusion of all otherwise eligible family members, without regard to the class of beneficiaries and the substantive entitlement contemplated by the parent Act, such restriction travels beyond the permissible limits of delegated legislation and cannot be sustained. This conclusion does not invalidate every provision of the amended Rule 4.10, nor does it prevent the competent authority from lawfully regulating the duration, manner and conditions of payment of family pension within the mandate of the Act.

Applying the above principles to the individual cases, it is evident that the claims of the petitioners have been declined principally by invoking the spouse-only restriction. Zahida Yasmeen, petitioner in W.P. No.26 of 2026, claims pension as an unmarried daughter; Mst. Nosheen Malik, petitioner in W.P. No.3426 of 2026, claims the same as a divorced daughter; whereas Mst. Falak Shah, petitioner in W.P. No.4050 of 2026, advances claims arising from the deaths of both her mother and father. Their respective marital statuses, by themselves, cannot furnish a lawful basis for rejecting their claims without examining the eligibility conditions prescribed under the governing statutory framework. The respondent departments were required to determine their claims in accordance with the Act and the applicable Rules, rather than treating the impugned spouse-only restriction or departmental clarification as conclusive.

A separate consideration arises in W.P. No.4050 of 2026, wherein the petitioner seeks family pension in respect of both her deceased parents, each of whom was a retired Government servant. This aspect is directly illuminated by the judgment of the august Supreme Court in Province of Punjab v. Kanwal Rashid (2021 SCMR 730), wherein the entitlement of an unmarried daughter to family pension in respect of both deceased parents was examined and the attempt to restrict such entitlement through a departmental clarification was disapproved. The august Supreme Court also held that receipt of family pension in respect of one deceased parent could not, merely by itself, be treated as an independently acquired regular source of income so as to disentitle the beneficiary from the pension admissible in respect of the other deceased parent. Accordingly, the claims arising from the deaths of the petitioner’s mother and father constitute two distinct pensionary entitlements and must be examined independently under the governing statutory framework. In the absence of an express statutory prohibition or a lawful condition governing concurrent receipt, the entitlement in respect of one parent cannot be presumed to extinguish the entitlement arising from the death of the other. The respondents shall, therefore, examine both claims in the light of the aforesaid binding precedent and the eligibility conditions applicable to each deceased pensioner and the petitioner.

In view of the foregoing discussion, the impugned refusals, insofar as they are founded exclusively upon the spouse-only restriction or the departmental clarification dated 30.05.2025, are not sustainable in law. The petitioners’ claims, however, involve individual questions concerning the fulfilment of the prescribed eligibility conditions, which are required to be examined by the competent pension authorities in the first instance. This Court, therefore, considers it appropriate to set aside the impugned refusals and remit the respective claims for fresh determination in accordance with the law declared herein, rather than directing payment of pension without prior verification of the statutory requirements.

For the foregoing reasons, all three constitutional petitions are allowed in the above terms. The clarification dated 30.05.2025, bearing No.FD-SR-III-4-237/2024, is declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect insofar as it purports to introduce an independent disqualification, alter the scope of Rule 4.10 or restrict an entitlement contrary to Section 18(2) Act. Likewise, the notifications dated 02.12.2024 and 20.08.2025, whereby amendments were introduced in Rule 4.10 of the Rules, are declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect only to the extent that their provisions are construed or applied so as to exclude otherwise eligible members of the deceased civil servant’s family in a manner inconsistent with Section 18(2) of the Act. Consequently, the impugned communications/orders declining the petitioners’ claims solely on the basis of the aforesaid unlawful restriction are hereby set aside.

The respective respondent departments are directed to reconsider and decide the respective claims of the petitioners afresh without treating them that she is a daughter, or the mere receipt of family pension in respect of another deceased parent, as an automatic disqualification. In W.P. No.4050 of 2026, the claims arising from the deaths of the petitioner’s mother and father shall be examined separately, including the question of concurrent receipt. The exercise shall be undertaken through speaking orders, after affording the petitioners an opportunity of hearing, preferably within a period of sixty days from receipt of a certified copy of this judgment. In the event that a petitioner is found entitled to family pension, the admissible pensionary benefits, together with consequential arrears, shall be released in accordance with law. (Syed Ahsan Raza Kazmi) Judge Approved for reporting. Judge Amjad/Azeem
